metadata.description: A place logs are accepted and kept: it offers intake over standard protocols, keeps what it receives for a declared number of days, and lets declared groups read it. A Base by the Base test (CLS-002): intake is standardized — syslog (RFC 5424, received over RFC 5425/5426/6587 transports) and OTLP — and every log store accepts one or both, so any of them can fill the order. Querying is not standardized (each store has its own query language), so this class says nothing about it. Retention and read access can differ by kind of record: a rule picks records by a criterion over their fields, the same kind a LogShipper filters with. Its senders are LogShipper records, which bind its published intake.

retention_days.description: The default retention, in days, for a record no rule in `rules` matches.

transport.description: The transport for that protocol — `tls`, `udp`, `tcp` or `relp` for syslog; `grpc` or `http` for OTLP.

intake.description: The intake the store must offer: each entry a protocol and a transport. A LogShipper can only bind a store that offers its protocol over its transport.

retention_days.description: Days to keep a record this rule picks. Absent keeps the store's default.

readers.description: The Groupings that may read what this rule picks, in place of the store's `readers`. Absent keeps the store's readers.

rules.description: Retention and read access by kind of record. Each rule picks records with `match`, a criterion over the log record (identifier-scheme §9.7), and sets `retention_days`, `readers`, or both, for what it picks. Rules are read in order and the first match wins; a record no rule matches gets the store's `retention_days` and its `readers` edges. A rule that sets neither gives what it picks those defaults, exempting it from the rules after it.

status.description: Realized health of the store (e.g. ready / degraded), as reported by discovery.

intake_endpoints.description: The realized intake: one entry per `intake` element, each { protocol, transport, address, port }. This is what a LogShipper's `sink` edge binds.

relationships.name: readers
relationships.description: The groups allowed to read the stored logs, unless a rule in `rules` says otherwise for what it picks. Access follows the same groupings that scope every other resource, so no store-local user list exists.

relationships.name: cluster
relationships.description: The cluster the store runs on, when it runs on one.

relationships.name: host
relationships.description: The machine the store runs on, when it runs on one directly.

context.purpose: Declares a log store by what it accepts, how long it keeps it, and who may read it.
context.plain_description: The request for a log store: how many days to keep messages by default, rules that keep some kinds longer or shorter or limit who reads them (authentication logs for a year, readable by security; debug lines for a week), which intake to offer (syslog over TLS, OTLP over HTTP, and so on), and which groups may read. Once realized, it publishes the address and port of each intake, and LogShipper records bind those. Which product stores the logs, and where its data lives, is the provider's business.
use_when: You need a central log store whose retention, intake and readers are declared and checkable.
not_for: Getting logs into it — that is LogShipper, one per source.
Querying — not standardized across stores, so not modelled here.
works_with: LogShipper — its senders, bound to its published intake.
